title: networking-streaming-overhead-synthesis-2026
content:
Executive summary:

This note summarizes a set of controlled experiments that profile networking and streaming overhead for our serving runtime. Goal: quantify the per-request and per-token costs introduced by transport (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC unary, gRPC streaming), chunking strategies, and proxies (Envoy) under both steady-state and backpressure scenarios. We recorded latency distributions (p50/p95/p99), throughput, CPU and socket metrics, and end-to-end token arrival times for streaming clients. The outcome is a set of pragmatic defaults and follow-up experiments to refine production routing policies.

Motivation and scope:
- Customers repeatedly surface tails and jitter for streaming responses; unclear whether root cause is app-level serialization, runtime scheduling, or transport/proxy behavior.
- We focus on network+transport overhead; model decode time and token generation variance is controlled via a synthetic token-emitter service (deterministic 2ms/token).
- Experiments run against dedicated GPU host to remove model variance; all numbers relate to transport and runtime network stack.

Testbed (hardware and baseline config):
- Server: r5a.large-ish VM (8 vCPU, 32GB), but tests repeated on GPU node with same network to confirm similar networking stack behavior. OS: Ubuntu 22.04. Kernel: 5.19.
- Client load generators: separate machines to avoid local scheduling interference. Tools: wrk2 (HTTP), ghz (gRPC unary), custom py-grpc-streamer for streaming patterns, iperf3 for link sanity.
- Proxy: Envoy v1.30 configured as HTTP/1.1 front for HTTP tests and HTTP/2 for gRPC passthrough.
- TLS: tests run both TLS enabled (letsencrypt certs via test CA) and plaintext; TLS increases CPU contribution and handshake costs — called out when relevant.
- Observability: node-exporter (CPU, net), eBPF tcp-timestamps, netstat snapshots, tcpdump for sample captures, go pprof when server in go, and strace for syscall-level verification.

Workloads and synthetic server behavior:
- Token emitter service: returns a streaming payload of N tokens where each token is emitted exactly 2ms after previous; token payload size controlled (default 32 bytes). This isolates transport latency and per-chunk overhead.
- Tests: unary-1 (HTTP POST sync full payload), unary-2 (gRPC unary blocking until complete), streaming-1 (HTTP chunked streaming), streaming-2 (gRPC streaming server-side), streaming-3 (gRPC bidi simplified where client sends a keepalive every X ms).
- Chunk sizes: small (128B), medium (1KB), large (8KB). Small = frequent system calls, large = fewer chunks but larger serialization cost.

Measurement methodology:
- For each combination (transport, chunk size, proxy on/off, TLS on/off) run a 5-minute trial with increasing concurrency steps: 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 concurrent streams/requests.
- Metrics captured per-trial: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency to first token, inter-token interval distribution, throughput (tokens/sec), server CPU (user/sys), network packets per second, syscall rate (write/send), socket queue lengths (ss -lt), and tail connection re-establishment rates.
- Repeat each trial 3x and report median.

Key findings (high level):
1) gRPC streaming (HTTP/2) generally shows lower per-token overhead than HTTP chunked streaming once rps > ~10 concurrent streams. Reason: HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces TCP connection churn and fewer per-chunk header bytes.
2) For very small chunks (<=128B) the syscall and Nagle interactions dominate: enabling TCP_NODELAY reduces tail for low-latency tokens but increases packet count and CPU.
3) Envoy in the path adds ~0.6–2.5ms p95 tail per token depending on config and buffer_watermarks; default Envoy config is too aggressive at buffering which increases inter-token delay when upstream emits small frequent writes.
4) TLS adds roughly +0.4–1.2ms p95 per token (mostly CPU and record boundary effects), but the handshake cost is amortized for long-lived streams.
5) gRPC unary vs HTTP unary: minimal difference for full-response requests, but unary patterns are poor fit for streaming semantics — unary forces server to buffer model output until completion unless server implements response streaming semantics.

Representative numbers (median of repeats, concurrency=25, token emitter=2ms/token, medium chunk=1KB):
- HTTP chunked streaming (no proxy, plaintext): p50 first-token: 4.8ms, p95 first-token: 12.6ms, inter-token median: 2.1ms, inter-token p95: 7.9ms, throughput: 48k tokens/sec aggregate.
- gRPC server stream (HTTP/2, no proxy, plaintext): p50 first-token: 3.6ms, p95 first-token: 9.0ms, inter-token median: 2.0ms, inter-token p95: 5.1ms, throughput: 52k tokens/sec aggregate.
- HTTP chunked through Envoy (default buffers): p95 inter-token: 15.4ms, observed batching at envoy side (envoy coalesced writes into 4–8KB bursts).
- gRPC streaming through Envoy (http2 bridge): p95 inter-token: 7.2ms, still higher than direct gRPC, but better than HTTP chunked via Envoy.

Detailed observations and root cause tracing notes:
- Syscall profile: small-chunk HTTP burst shows high write(2) rate (~12k syscalls/sec at concurrency=50). Each write triggered a sendmmsg small packet which correlated with kernel tcp push/timestamp behavior.
- Nagle/TCP_NODELAY: with Nagle enabled small writes were aggregated at kernel level, producing added latency spikes around 5–15ms at p95; enabling TCP_NODELAY removed aggregation but increased packet-per-token (and CPU).
- Envoy buffering: default http1/stream idle and watermarks led Envoy to accumulate several small writes before flushing. Adjusting upstream_flush_delay_ms and per-connection buffer settings reduced observed coalescing. Patch experiment: setting upstream_flush_delay_ms=1ms and lowering per-connection buffer produced dramatic reductions in p95 inter-token latency for HTTP chunked (from 15.4ms -> 6.2ms).
- HTTP/1.1 upgrade: using HTTP/1.1 with chunked and connection reuse still underperformed compared to HTTP/2 gRPC streaming for multiplexed scenarios due to head-of-line blocking when multiple concurrent streams per connection were used.
- Keepalives and connection reuse: frequent connection setup (no keepalive) penalized short-lived unary flows heavily; long-lived streaming connections amortize TLS and handshake costs.

Experiment-specific notes and commands (repro steps):
- Token emitter server (Go pseudo):
  go run ./cmd/token-emitter --emit-ms=2 --size=32 --mode=grpc-stream --port=8085
- gRPC client load (ghz):
  ghz --proto proto/stream.proto --call StreamService.Emit --concurrency 25 --connections 25 --rps 0 --insecure --duration 300s target:8085
- HTTP chunked generator (wrk2-based): custom lua body streamer that issues chunked writes every 2ms matching emitter cadence.
- Envoy sample snapshot: envoy configs used are attached in PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/834 (see envoy/streaming-config.yaml)
- Packet capture sanity: tcpdump -i eth0 -w trial1.pcap port 8085 (sample pcap attached to linked artifacts)

Practical recommendations (defaults to adopt in product):
1) Expose gRPC streaming as the preferred production streaming surface: it consistently has lower per-token inter-arrival tail and fewer corner cases with proxies when using HTTP/2.
2) When HTTP chunked must be supported (legacy customers), document and ship a recommended Envoy tuning snippet: lower upstream_flush_delay_ms, tighten buffer_watermarks, and enable per-stream flush heuristics.
3) Default server-side to emit slightly larger chunk boundaries (e.g., 512–1024B) for small token payloads to reduce syscall overhead while keeping token latency acceptable. Make chunk-size adaptive: if inter-token interval < 1.5ms group tokens into 512B chunks.
4) Expose an opt-in TCP_NODELAY telemetry toggle: recommend for ultra-low latency customers but warn about increased CPU/packet-costs.
5) TLS: leave enabled by default for hosted, but document the observed +0.5–1ms per-token overhead and recommend long-lived streams to amortize.

Open questions & follow-ups:
- Probe kernel-bypass options (AF_XDP) or coalesced sendmmsg improvements to reduce syscall overhead for extreme tail cases.
- Repeat tests over cloud providers with different virtual NIC implementations (AWS ENA vs GCE vs Azure) — early runs show AWS ENA can reduce p95 by ~10–20% in the small-chunk regime.
- Memory-pressure interactions: run high memory GC churn server builds to measure pause amplification on inter-token timing (esp. Java/Python runtimes).
- Client library ergonomics: provide an official JS/Go/py streaming client that implements optimal chunking, keepalives, and backoff to minimize application-level jitter.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting checklist for customer reports of streaming jitter:
- Is runtime emitting tokens < 2ms apart? If yes, likely kernel/syscall dominated — suggest batch tokens into 512–1KB chunks.
- Is there Envoy in the path? Ask for envoy config; check buffer_watermarks and upstream_flush_delay_ms.
- Are client connections reused? If not, handshake penalties may dominate — recommend keepalive or persistent stream.
- Check TCP_NODELAY setting on client socket. Optionally toggle to measure difference.
- Capture a small pcap of a reported slow stream; look for coalesced packets and delayed PSH flags.

- Draft a short internal playbook and an external support KB entry describing Envoy tuning and recommended client settings.

Notes to reviewer:
- I left raw pcap and eBPF traces attached to the PR. The numbers above are median-of-medians across runs but variations remain in p99; please review envoy config patch for safety with large-scale traffic.

End of note.
